newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka economy on track, Central Bank deputy says.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka economy on track, Central Bank deputy says.

text.p: Sri Lanka's economy is on track and gross domestic product (GDP) growth should bounce back to six percent this year from 3.8 percent in 1996, the deputy governor of the Central Bank said on Thursday.

"We're reasonably confident the economy is on track, barring any unforeseen circumstances," S. Easparathasan told Reuters in an interview. "I believe all the indicators are that the markets perceive that the positive developments are here to stay."
Easparathasan said sustained growth of seven to eight percent was possible for the Indian Ocean island in the medium term.
"The economy showed a fair degree of resilience, mainly in the latter half of 1996," he said.
"Going on how things picked up in the second half of 1996 and what is coming out of the first quarter of 1997, one has justifiable reason to be satisfied with the performance so far."
The Central Bank said in its annual report released on Wednesday that GDP growth last year fell to 3.8 percent from 5.5 percent in 1995 mainly because of war and drought.
Easparathasan said there was no indication so far that defence spending would exceed the 44 billion rupees ($743 million) budgeted for this year.
"Most of the military hardware requirements have been built into the budget," he said.

The government says more than 50,000 people have been killed in the war against the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam rebels, who are fighting for an independent homeland for minority Tamils in the north and east. The war is into its 14th year.
Last year, defence spending reached 48 billion rupees from the original allocation of 33.9 billion because of an escalation in fighting.
Easparathasan also said Sri Lanka's annual average inflation as measured by the consumer price index was seen falling to 10 percent this year from 15.9 percent in 1996.
Inflationary pressures of 1996 had not been seen in the first quarter of this year, he said.
The report said annual average inflation rose sharply in 1996 because of higher food costs after international wheat prices shot up.
Easparathasan said the Sri Lankan rupee would stabilise soon, despite its recent fall of just over two percent against the dollar in the past five weeks.
"The exchange rate is largely a market-determined rate, and with the outlook on the macro-economic fundamentals strong, I would really say that it will soon stabilise itself," he said.
The Sri Lankan rupee was quoted at 59.20 to the dollar on Wednesday, 2.35 percent lower than 57.84 in late March. The forex market was closed for the May Day holiday on Thursday.
Easparathasan said the Central Bank had no plans to intervene in the market. ($1 = 59.2 rupees)
